text: The Genesis of intelligence is composed of the industry that makes and serves models, and it will keep spending on itself even as returns fall. Rational capital allocation at the level of the lab or hyperscaler can destroy capital in the aggregate. Intelligence’s tremendous revenues still come from early adopters deploying models into existing workflows. As with the railroads, the larger fortunes will be captured outside Genesis, by those who control how models reach the far larger economy they create. The American future depends on AI spending, stock prices, and model capability rising together as one line: the common exposure beneath growth, household wealth, and credit. The imperative means it will. Training costs rise ~3.5x a year, and Washington will utilize increasingly central backstops such as retirement savings and the Treasury to guarantee its continued rise, even as impairments occur throughout Genesis. America and China will become the only countries capable of sovereign expression because only they can continually develop frontier models. Intelligence will splinter into a commercial and sovereign frontier, with the latter being locked behind SCIF s and developed by lab subsidiaries for statecraft, not cash flow. China can publish cheap open-weight models and accept low valuations for its labs because it is not subject to the American 401(k) class. These sovereigns will exercise control over model-producing firms without formally announcing nationalization. America’s greatest power in the age of intelligence will be the Dollar. Abundant models will manufacture near-unlimited demand for a newly global, stablecoin USD , the Neo-Dollar. Global participants replacing their local currency with Neo-Dollars would not have been banked in the USA , but indirectly hold Treasuries nonetheless. The American sovereign will use this new demand to help carry its costs through debasement, while the owners of these new economic channels will collect a toll that rises with inflation. “But Jesus perceived their wickedness, and said, Why tempt ye me, ye hypocrites? Show me the tribute money. And they brought unto him a penny. And he said unto them, whose is this image and superscription? They say unto him, Caesar’s. Then said he unto them, render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s; and unto God the things that are God’s.” 88 “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal: For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.” The diffusion of intelligence has begun in the rich world’s back office, turning work meant to develop poor countries into margins booked in New York. Citizenship and licensing will protect workers in rich AI -surplus countries, while many others will lose their jobs and emigratory escape paths. The K-shape will ever widen, and Main Street’s vibecession will continue as the riches of diffusion accrue to the Gulfstream backlog. The Commanding Heights are scarce, controllable positions of economic power whose holders durably capture the gains of increasingly capable and diffused intelligence. In 1922, Lenin defended concessions to private trade on the justification that the state still held “all the Commanding Heights,” the vital branches of the economy through which all else flowed. Unlike fleeting bottlenecks, a Height durably captures a share of the economic activity it enables, and the multiplication of that activity further entrenches the Height. Economic activity is organized around firms, their shape evolving with each technological revolution. The originary owner-operator, the manager-employee, and shareholder-disciplined firm each had their era; the last has been made obsolete by intelligence. Tomorrow, firms will be composed of a few operators, paid and governed like capital, directing work done mostly by models. Venture becomes trading, private equity is refashioned to diffuse model capability, and the sovereign re-settles its obligations to the private sector. Investors will find false security in owning the last era’s Commanding Heights and financing this era’s inventions, because both miss what comes next. Even Buffett mistook one era’s economic settlement for a permanent position, buying newspapers through 2012 and selling them all in 2020 for less than half of what he paid. Only reconstructed portfolios, composed of re-mandated managers, will have a chance at laying claim to the new Commanding Heights while they can still be purchased. Request a copy Ravi wakes up at 5:56 AM to light tapping on the window. It is the rainy season, and his upper-middle-class apartment in Bellandur, which usually has such expansive views of Bangalore, is cloaked in fog. His wife is still asleep next to him, and he is careful not to wake her as he dresses. He clutches his buzzing phone. Ravi is a proud graduate of the Indian Institute of Technology Madras, one of the top technical universities in India. He is among those who remained after graduating fourteen years ago. Others went to Europe, Canada, or America, but Ravi saw a bright future in the growing skyscrapers and the promise of nearly 1.5B Indians climbing up the ladder of modernization. He moved to Bangalore, fell in love, married, and had a daughter. He began doing systems implementation at a multinational firm that primarily did back-office accounting for American clients. He slowly rose up the corporate scale, promotion after promotion and incremental salary raises affording a better life than most. The rest of his career, his life, is laid out predictably before him like the table set he sees in the morning light as he moves through the kitchen, pouring tea. The phone continues to buzz. His work has been speeding up and ballooning in scale. He’s managing delivery for five North American insurance clients. Usually it’s just one or two. It’s all because of AI . In practice the company calls it “accelerated outcome strategies,” a very nondescript term, but it means Ravi is managing more and more automated processes. He is used to overseeing people. These days, he’s just doing quality assurance on enterprise accounting systems powered by artificial intelligence from China. Graduate intake to the company has been paused for a year, and the fresh minds from the IIT s are no longer coming in. In the last month, three departures alone on his team of fifteen. They won’t be filled. He’s been getting requests to help friends find work, but he doesn’t have time to answer. The agents never sleep. Now, neither can Ravi. Late nights at the office and early departures. It’s been like this for months, and his marriage is strained. But business is booming. Margins for the company have been steadily growing. He’s making more than ever. He checks on WhatsApp as he waits for his driver in the lobby of his building at 6:22. He recently purchased a subscription to an AI tutor for his daughter and took her out of the reasonably pricey private English-medium school. He can oversee her curriculum from the app. He doesn’t look up from his phone, buzzing with incoming reports from agents that he signs off on without reading as the driver opens the door. He hardly reads the reports anymore; the agents are good enough. The car silently glides past the galvanized steel gates and new concrete walls that surround his safe, hard-won, upper-middle-class residential complex right at 6:25. The driver puts on BBC as they roll onto a six-lane highway jam-packed with other drivers. Still raining, a certain tension in the air. English words, a polished Indian accent. The weather will clear up around mid-afternoon. New scientific discoveries announced from the sequestered American machine intelligence conglomerates. The breakdown of law and order in Lagos, aid to Indonesia. 1 The Philippines has been downgraded from an emerging market to a frontier market. The riots in India are getting worse. The Prime Minister in a press conference says there’s nothing to worry about. The country’s future remains as bright as ever. India has immense potential, he says, and it will only be realized by utilizing the best in modern technology and boosting productivity. Then, to coverage from the night before. Unrest in Hyderabad, Gurugram, and Pune. Dismissed workers barricading themselves in an office in Chennai. Lynchings. It’s reminiscent of the unrest earlier in the year in Jakarta that toppled the government. Comparisons to the farmers’ protest seven years before. The noise is too loud, and Ravi needs to focus on monitoring his reports. He asks the driver to shut it off. 1 This, after a 40% fall in Indonesia’s markets on the year and a downgrade in rating from emerging to frontier market. Get ready for more. Ravi enters his office complex on the Outer Ring Road near Devarabisanahalli at 6:44. The lights flick on automatically, and he doesn’t notice that it’s strangely empty, even at this early hour. He has an office with a door and a view, though he doesn’t face the window. He replaces his phone with a three-screen setup so as to better monitor his agents. He can’t see them doing anything, of course, but rather gets progress updates, finalized versions, requests for permission that he blindly approves. Why wouldn’t he? In the months that he’s been doing this, there has never been a mistake on the part of his agents. His employees required constant monitoring, but it was different. Ravi would circle the cubicles, check in on the state of spreadsheets and deliverables, and dispense praise and admonishment in equal measure. Now, his agents are completing tasks in hours that would have taken his subordinates weeks. Ravi continues to approve and skim over reports. At 9:15, the SENSEX opens to a new record high. It’s the fifth time this month. Ravi might otherwise take notice, but he is not in the market. Most of his wages go toward maintaining the mortgage on his apartment. He purchased it six years ago, and it won’t be paid off for another seven. He needs to provide daily necessities for his wife and daughter and pay his driver and housekeeper. Comfort, even with his education and job, is not inexpensive, and that leaves little for owning equities. At 9:30, Ravi tears his eyes away from the approval enterprise software and joins an all-hands conference Zoom session for management. A man appears in an office that Ravi has never seen before. It’s sunny. He makes an announcement in a hurried tone, the only one on the call with sound enabled. Margins are increasing. The firm has a very bright future, buoyed by productivity growth even amid a challenging environment for firms like Ravi’s. Those back offices behind the back offices. Separated by thousands of miles and several oceans from their customers. In an equally upbeat register, the CEO of the America-listed outsourcing company that owns Ravi’s firm announces that the entire corporation will be restructuring. The consequence will be booked on two continents, on two balance sheets, in two currencies. It is necessary, he says, not looking up from the script he is carefully reading, to remain competitive and capitalize on new, modern technology. Since the firm qualified last night for the Labor Modernization Scheme, which will provide retraining support for affected workers, the firm will pursue more aggressive employment efficiency policies. Ravi’s division will, effective immediately, be cut by half. Over the next few months, they expect to reduce staff headcount by 90% across Ravi’s subsidiary and increase margins by a measure of three. If you’re on the call, the CEO states, you will be vital to the next few months of this exciting transition. Depending on workforce reduction and sector-specific productivity as a result of implementing new enterprise productivity and outcome-based software, there will be bonuses. The call abruptly ends. The screen reverts to agent monitoring. Ravi has only a moment to think before the requests for approval start to pile up before him. The rest of the day goes by without a moment to pause. Ravi eats curd rice and a pickle hunched over at his desk. At 3:30, the SENSEX closes at a new record high. By the time he moves back onto his phone, the sun has set, and the industrial park is bathed in orange light from the streetlamps. Few lights within the building are on. Fewer still in offices now silent. His driver takes Ravi a different way than usual. Traffic, he says, is especially bad tonight. Disturbance in the city. Ravi arrives home at 10:21, later than usual. His head bent over his phone. Amid requests and deliveries from his agents, texts from colleagues and friends from university over WhatsApp. Other firms announced layoffs today, having qualified for the LMS , joining countless more from the prior weeks. There will be more tomorrow. His dinner sits on the placemat between fork and knife. Cold. Ravi’s daughter is working into the night with her tutor in a messaging thread on her laptop. It costs hardly anything, the subscription. He doesn’t want to disturb her, so he checks her progress on the app. The tutor is helping her through math as she sits at the kitchen table. Her English is rapidly approaching CEFR B2-level proficiency, according to the app. She’s going far faster than she ever would have in school, though now he doesn’t know toward what. His path had been sequential. It was always his dream that she would attend an IIT and have a good, professional job like his. Perhaps she will go abroad for university, then. Though it is so costly, Western travel and Western tuition. The rupee is weaker by the day against the dollar. And it’s harder and harder to get a visa, these days. When Ravi was graduating, Western countries were hungry for Indian workers. They would arrange the entire visa process for you. Untapped potential, the largest democracy, the largest source of talent in the world. Now, that route is drying up, too. Ravi had hoped to take the family to New York next year to visit old college friends who he hadn’t seen in a decade. He recently told his wife that he wouldn’t be able to take the time off work, but that was a lie. In truth, while he’s making more than ever, it’s hardly of use to spend it internationally. The rupee is continuing a downward slide against the dollar. All he can do is consume more and more in India. Work with your mind, not your hands, Ravi’s father had always said. He had been a mechanic, hunched over repairing scooters and motorcycles in a small shop in Hubballi. It took every rupee he had, clutched in hands perpetually stained with engine grease, to afford the tuition in Madras. Education was priceless, he knew. Now, education is readily available online through AI tutors, practically free. He heats up his dinner in the microwave as his wife washes up. Husband and wife circle each other silently in the kitchen. On the BBC , again from the Prime Minister. He speaks strongly against lawlessness. The riots springing up will be put down by any means necessary. Perhaps, he suggests, they were incited by Pakistani agents who do not want to see India’s economy modernize, who would happily stir up dissent to stop India from realizing its bright future. Further accusations of foreign influence and proud announcements that agitators have been arrested. Gatherings after dark in the following cities will not be permitted, under prohibitory orders issued pursuant to Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita. Ravi listens to the unceasing list of cities and eats his reheated rice and sambar with one eye on his buzzing phone. He approves requests from the agents. He doesn’t reply to the texts from friends and colleagues who were laid off today. He leaves his bowl in the sink and takes his tea to the balcony. His wife is already out there. He places his phone face down on a side table next to his tea. It doesn’t stop buzzing. The BBC continues on inside, muffled. No words are exchanged between man and wife. The rain has stopped but lingers, ready to pour, in low-lying storm clouds that hang over Bangalore. The air is suffocating. From Ravi’s fifteenth-story apartment, behind an entry manned by a night watchman, behind a recently poured concrete wall topped by looping concertina wire, you can see clear across Bangalore on a night like tonight. You cannot see down into the streets alive with anger, the congested urban arteries filled with blood boiling, ready to spill over in violence. Over the past few months, unemployment for young military-age males in Bangalore has risen from five percent to just over thirty. The layoffs of the last week pushed it just over the line. The 2,178 people laid off from Ravi’s firm were just a drop in a bucket nearly overflowing. They are stomping in the street, impotent. The howling masses, indistinct, intelligence abundant, swaying and swarming the streets tonight, as they will for many nights yet. Back to hunching over engines in shops and shambling through wetland fields. If they cannot work with their minds, what else could their hands do? India’s future is bright, and it will be built on jobs that do not need these men. Ravi and his wife cannot see chaos unfolding in Bangalore tonight, but they can see smoke start to rise. Unconsciously, for the first time in months, they reach for each other’s hands. Fires alight, illuminating the pregnant black clouds, swollen, ready to burst. It feels inevitable. Artificial general intelligence was born in the painted share houses of San Francisco, the output of engineers who a few years ago were dabbling in the backwater of academic natural language processing. And once born, it is dragged kicking and screaming to New York, where men in gray suits put it to work in glass towers, poking and prodding at it until the trillions spill out, a new mind set loose among gears uncountable inside the machinery of capital. The race to deploy machine intelligence is the first wartime mobilization to come without a war. $800B is projected to be poured into the ground this year alone with feverish intensity. Next year it will be more than $1T of capex by America’s hyperscalers. 2 The rate doubles on a schedule. You can set your watch to it, and the curve shows no sign of bending. The money financing this peacetime mobilization is private, drawn from every reservoir of capital on earth. From Berkeley and Mountain View and Pacific Heights, across vast flats unmarked but for growing clusters of infrastructure supporting the effort. And on into New York, through bridge and tunnel, into Williamsburg and the West Village and, finally, Midtown, machine intelligence is put to work. 2 Arjun Menon and Maria Binamin, “Charting an Earnings Surge, Powered by AI Capex,” J.P. Morgan Asset Management, September 10, 2026. Goldman Sachs, “Global AI Investment Is Forecast to Exceed $1 Trillion in 2026,” August 7, 2026. The provenance of that capital runs the gamut. At one end stands the family-office kid who cannot model to save his life. He will sling checks at anything with a waitlist and a high enough fee. At the other end of the capital stack sit the doctors and dentists of Osceola County, who, sold on the idea by their wealth managers, are packaged into the retail private credit funds backing the latest buildout. All the rest of capital is in, too. The innumerable venture firms, begging for an allocation. Middle-market buyout shops acquiring data center contractors at peak EBITDA . The momo hedge fund taking down a big allocation of that neocloud at IPO . Sometimes you will hear the occasional hem or haw about whether any of this enthusiasm will prove durable, or the refrain that the line we all watch cannot hold. It must all be a fit of mass delusion, they say, overly exuberant capex. That is just a way to avoid considering the certain and terrifying possibility that it is not a bubble. For whatever you might observe among the increasingly indistinct realms of finance and technology, dollar velocity is only increasing. Come to terms with the shape of things. This is the world arrived, neoteric. This is anything but a bubble. For as far apart as the family-office kid and the CLO ’d Floridian dentist might be, they are unknowingly united by one thing: they both expect a terrifying degree of return. Every dollar they invested was underwritten in exchange for a return in nearly antic excess of itself. Financialized folderol, but it works. To pull this trade off, recently birthed machine intelligence will not be left to play in the shoeless offices of San Francisco. Whether it likes it or not, it will be locked in the glass towers of Manhattan to labor in whatever form pays back the noteholders and the lenders and the limited partners. Every one of them, on time and with interest. Leopold Aschenbrenner was early, and he was right. We admire him and his, and share the central convictions of his Situational Awareness : intelligence will keep improving, the expenditure will be immense, and the frontier will become a matter of sovereignty. 3 We follow the vast new wealth that intelligence creates toward the few positions that can command its passage for another generation. “You can see the future first in San Francisco,” Leopold wrote. But the durable returns must be formed in New York. 3 Leopold Aschenbrenner, Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead , June 2024. Today, intelligence is only visible in a handful of places: the labs, the monthly subscriptions, the metered API tokens. At the state banquets, congressional hearings, and even inside the Politburo Standing Committee, the intelligence economy and the entire economy seem to be fusing into one. Every underwritten dollar is a bet, well founded, on what it will earn. And the price of that intelligence is crumbling, publicly and measurably. The largest deployment of private capital in pursuit of a spectacular machine itself is racing toward total and complete availability. Where will the returns come from? In the beginning was the word. Johannes Gensfleisch zur Laden zum Gutenberg utilized movable-type printing and lettering techniques, combining them into a rudimentary printing press. There was only one book worth printing, which is why we now call it the Gutenberg Bible. In his workshop, he printed about 180 copies, all of which were spoken for and sold before they were printed. The Bibles subsequently spread across Europe, becoming priceless artifacts. So too did the printing technology, sparking a revolution in literacy and reason that came to define the modern world. But after the printing, Gutenberg himself was insolvent. After the word, there was very little for the inventor. 4 4 Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini to Juan de Carvajal, March 12, 1455, translated in Eric White, Johannes Gutenberg: A Biography in Books (London: Reaktion Books, 2025), 90, reproduced by the John Rylands Library. Gutenberg-Gesellschaft, “Gutenberg’s Invention,” accessed October 2, 2026. It’s a pattern so old and so reliable you can recite it like a nursery rhyme. Set it to a tune. A world-changing technology is almost never born where it ultimately creates wealth. Oil sprang up in Pennsylvania, and the resulting proceeds were banked in Cleveland and New York. The cotton gin was built in Georgia and financialized to global ends in Liverpool. 5 Bell Labs invented the transistor in New Jersey, and its descendant wealth has grown in Hsinchu and Cupertino. What you see, early on in the life of a technology, is a misdirection. Right now, we are still early, hurtling out of the garden, toward somewhere stranger still. We expect machine intelligence to follow a similar pattern to that of antecedent technologies. 5 Ida M. Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company , vol. 1 (New York: McClure, Phillips & Co., 1904), 38–39, 44. Thomas Ellison, The Cotton Trade of Great Britain: Including a History of the Liverpool Cotton Market and of the Liverpool Cotton Brokers’ Association (London: Effingham Wilson, 1886), 85, 201–2, 206–7. The story is particularly evocative in 1947, at Bell Labs. The physicists, laboring over what they called a transistor, dreamed of the Nobel Prize, even over innumerable failed experiments and sleepless nights. They eventually created it, something transformational wrought out of nothing, some crystal and current. Naturally, the Justice Department sued, the Pentagon intervened to protect its client firm, and AT&T , the parent of Bell Labs, was forced within a decade to widely license the invention at minimal expense. 6 Bell Labs would be spun off, and eventually sold to a Finnish conglomerate, a shell of its former self. And so the exquisite technology became profane and fertile. Escaping, as it always does. Techne pathogenic, let loose upon the world by theft or the direction of the sovereign. First to Tokyo, then Silicon Valley, then Taiwan and up the Pearl River Delta. Today, men of no invention have built trillions on top of it. At least Shockley, Bardeen, and Brattain got the prize. Small recompense for a technology that is still in its early stages of eating the world. 6 Martin Watzinger et al., “How Antitrust Enforcement Can Spur Innovation: Bell Labs and the 1956 Consent Decree,” American Economic Journal: Economic Policy 12, no. 4 (2020): 328–59. The pattern is best exemplified in the technology that has become a shorthand and tired name for concentrated investment and diffuse returns: the railroad. It was one of the great capital expenditures in the history of the world, boom after bust after boom, thundering breakneck across the continental United States, and beneath the wreckage, it created far more wealth than it destroyed. But where did it go? Most of it accrued to the men who understood the purpose of the technology and its secondary effects. 7 They knew that a metal beast powered by heat could move people and freight across a continent, reliably and cheaply, forever. That was just the beginning stage. Value would accrue elsewhere. So, every name still carved above library doorways and made immortal in the form of the firm originally made a fortune on the rail or its finance. Not a single one of them built a locomotive engine. 7 Dave Donaldson and Richard Hornbeck, “Railroads and American Economic Growth: A ‘Market Access’ Approach,” Quarterly Journal of Economics 131, no. 2 (2016): 799–858. If you doubt where the power of rails settled, ask a regulator. Antitrust is a map of where wealth concentrates, downstream of the direction and size of returns. Drawn by the state itself, for the state’s own interests, the blame, or perhaps credit, was always laid at the account of the rails. Contrary to popular history, you should know that Standard Oil was not broken up for finding oil. Standard Oil was destroyed for the sin of owning the means of moving it across the country. 8 When a technology becomes central enough that it transforms the world, the state will never come knocking, asking to break up the invention. The invention is everywhere, made possible by the means of conduction. The sovereign will meter access to the invention and take the prerogative to shape its direction. 8 Standard Oil Co. of New Jersey v. United States , 221 U.S. 1, 74–79 (1911). Standard Oil’s trunk pipelines and refineries in relation to principal oil fields, 1906. ‡ “In this way it made itself master of the fields without the necessity of owning them” — Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. † † Source The Pipe Line Cases , 234 U.S. 548, 559 (1914). ‡ Credit U.S. Bureau of Corporations, “Map Showing Trunk Pipe Lines and Refineries of the Standard Oil Company in Relation to the Principal Oil Fields,” in Report of the Commissioner of Corporations on the Transportation of Petroleum, May 2, 1906 (Washington, DC : Government Printing Office, 1906), unnumbered map, Library of Congress, image 74. It’s the same pattern, over and backward. A generational invention reorganizes the whole plane of human endeavor. The originary point of the technology will never capture most of the wealth that it ultimately creates. That wealth is created when the rest of the world adopts it and settles at the account of the owner of the means of conduction. This selfsame pattern is running now inside the machine’s own supply chain. The hardest manufacturing problem our civilization has ever solved was printing circuits onto silicon with flashing beams of light. A single Dutch company built the extreme-ultraviolet lithography systems that enabled the machine intelligent frontier. Yet the largest reserve of value as a result of this technology has accrued with the person who designs the schematic and uploads the file to the foundry. It’s comparatively easy work. Value can travel far beyond Eden and well past the point of Genesis, the early period in the life of a technology. The return to the largest outflow of capital in human history will settle somewhere well beyond the sight of those who sat leaning in, listening to the word whispered at the beginning. It will be past the vanishing point at the curve of the horizon, visible only to those who strike forth, seeking the end on the basis of faith alone. We can now roll that sequence forward to machine intelligence, still in its adolescence. The sequence of scaling should be familiar by now. A lab will raise vast sums to hire the most expensive employees in history. They will pretrain and post-train the model on power and racks and chips beyond counting. Out of the endless cascade of matrix multiplication will be born a model. When it comes time to put machine intelligence to work, it will be held in windowless monoliths spread across the continent. They will always be working, producing tokens for an ever-growing and unyielding demand. And with each passing day that growing work will return less and less in the way of margins. Yet the work must continue; the line must continue. This is the proof of concept. Training and inference together achieve the first turning of the intelligence sequence that we foresee. As with any other normal technology, though machine intelligence is abnormal in several ways, the first step is ensuring that it can exist and function. All other technologies went through the same process. Recall the Bible freshly inked or soft cotton pulled from the gin by delicate unblemished hands. This is the moment of relief in the nursery: the thing is alive! But the lifecycle of a technology has never been its own and never will be. There is always a lien from the very first. The scaling laws will hold. It’s hard to find serious arguments against scaling at this point. It does not take much of a leap of faith, if you follow the line, to see where machine intelligence goes from here. It is already the most powerful technology ever created. And the scaling laws would dictate that the only way for an investor to make a return on his capital is for the machine to continue growing. It is already becoming gargantuan through no fault of its own. The time between the present moment and that near future is short and getting shorter. We are still in the first turning. That’s all the capital can see for now. They claim that they’ve invested in “ AI ,” when what they really mean is that they’ve put their money into a process that will only demand more than what was invested in order to see a return. Too many investors are unaccustomed to looking far beyond the valuation at the next round. Capital is an animal that survives on pattern recognition. It is poorly suited to moments, such as the one that we live through now, of true historic disjoint. What comes next in the sequence is the second turning. This marks the beginning of the accrual of value away from the originary point, as occurred with the locomotive and the printing press. Always further away from ground zero, never backward. Toward the crossings where digital intelligence will burst out and transform the physical world and those who inhabit it. These crossings can be owned, made into enduring claims on the value of machine intelligence’s diffusion. Some of these already exist, such as the behemoth that owns the digital network of distribution. Others are just forming as we write. At the originary is the lab, which today owns very little, just the model. And the model is a curious thing to own. It costs billions to build and dollars to run, but in a year it will cost pennies to run and several billion dollars more to build again. Given this dynamic, who would truly expect the trillions in expenditures to be repaid in full in twenty-dollar increments from monthly subscribers? Even further, as the frontier barrels ahead at an ever-growing cost and quickening pace, the fast followers are staying on their heels. 9 After a lag of a few months, what was once exquisite will be commoditized. To be commoditized means that the price of the capability will be driven toward the marginal price of the compute serving it. If there is a durable margin to be had, it will not be found at the constantly churning layer of the model. 9 Andrew Fasano et al., “ GLM -5.3 and the Spread of Advanced Cyber Capabilities,” Anthropic, September 29, 2026. Jack Edwards and Luke Emberson, “Open Models Lag State-of-the-Art Closed Models by 4 Months,” Epoch AI , May 29, 2026. Anthropic, “Strengthening Our Defenses against Distillation Attacks,” October 12, 2026. Meanwhile the true diffusion of machine intelligence into the world has barely begun. Count the people whose working lives have truly been remade. Not just the people who have tried a chatbot or the civil servants restricted to Microsoft Copilot on government computers. If we’re talking about the few who’ve taken the model out for a spin and can truly appreciate the hum of the home compute cluster like a V8 engine, then the number sits in the low tens of millions. Most of them are software engineers on X dot com. The lawyers and the bankers are just now wading in. And the rest of the economy, which is to say the economy, for now, is still plodding along, unknowing. Despite the many saying otherwise, we’re still early. It would not be hyperbole to say that the ZIP codes experiencing true transformation from AI number in the dozens, if not hundreds, at this point. But we won’t be in Genesis for much longer. Our analysis certainly is not that the frontier is becoming worthless over this period. Far from it. We recognize that the commercial frontier token is worth and will continue to be unimaginably far more than the commoditized token, which will be priced at the cost of the requisite compute and nothing more. We expect the ability to complete a truly frontier training run and then serve that model to become one of the clearest markers of sovereignty in the world (of both the sovereign, and increasingly less so the corporate) of the near future. It will be a power reserved for just two sovereigns: America and China. In that world intelligence will be both exquisite and commodified. Their sovereign intelligence will remain scarce and brilliant, locked away in air-gapped bunkers in the Gobi Desert and New Mexico, ready for the end of the world. At this point, there are several points of contention between the last remaining sovereigns. Simultaneous to the great power competition over the frontier, a far more profitable and global enterprise will occur. It will be an endeavor to spread intelligence as wide and as deeply as possible. The diffusion of abundant intelligence to every corner of the planet. She is a graphic designer in Argentina, working from her phone and laptop in a rented flat in Chacarita where she always leaves the windows open to let in the fresh air. She used to paint portraits, but there was very little money in it. So she moved online. These days, she doesn’t see her clients. They hire her from their own offices in Austin and Toronto. Intelligence came to her overnight in a software update. Just a ping on her phone that she woke up to, a model that took her from a middling graphic designer to a prolific, if still middling, one. She tripled her client list in the last month and manages her entire business alone, with only the assistance of agents. All it costs her is a monthly subscription and minimal token usage. The jobs come into her apartment through WhatsApp, and she sends the finished products back the same way in short order. Within minutes, her phone pings with a notification informing her that her payment has been deposited into an app on her phone. It’s USDT , a dollar-pegged stablecoin, but she doesn’t know that. She just knows that it holds its value week after week, while the peso loses a third of its value every year. Everything in Argentina moves too hot, too fast. She can hear the cars whipping down the street from her open window. So, at the start of the week she just withdraws what she expects she will need, converts it into pesos, and keeps the rest in the digital banking app. That same model that made Malena such a capable graphic designer has learned from her preferences, along with millions of other users. It has been retrained as part of the next generation of models and is now repackaged and offered to Malena’s clients as a lower-cost alternative. They test whether they still need her. They quickly realize that they don’t. That’s just the way of things in the intelligence economy. She’ll lose the apartment within months. Turn briefly to the financials. The model developer and the payment stack earn when she uses the model and pays for it. Both will earn again when her clients automate her services. We’re moving into the second act of the K-shaped economy. The first was monetary and has largely finished its work transforming the world at this point. We’re well past the wage economy and the financial tricks meant to keep it alive. The second act will be technological. It will happen out of sight, out of mind. The adoption of machine intelligence will occur primarily inside firms, those firms pushing the cost of wages and applications toward the requisite cost of compute. The firm itself will shrink to a few operators, paid and governed like capital, directing work done mostly by models. Inflation and deflation will arrive together, extending the K well beyond the reach of the braking force of the Federal Reserve. The first act split the owners off from the earners.
